clue.text: Shout out for Hearts in matches, yelling "Goal"

parts.note: pro is the Latin for 'for', as in pro-Europe or the pros and cons

indicators.note: The heart of a word is the letter sitting dead centre, and both words named beside it have seven letters, so each gives up its fourth.

parts.note: seven letters, so the middle one is the fourth
another seven-letter word giving up its middle letter the same way
a goal is what you aim at, the target you set yourself

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is football commentary, so 'Hearts' looks like the Edinburgh club Heart of Midlothian. It is really the anatomical sense: the very centre of a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shout out -> PROCLAIM: to proclaim is to announce something publicly and at volume, which is shouting it out rather than merely saying it.

clue.text: Become thinner? Order a fryer

indicators.note: To order a set of things is to put them in an arrangement of your choosing, and the setter wants one other than the arrangement printed.

parts.note: six letters across the two words, to be reassembled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Order a fryer' reads as a line from a catering catalogue, which is what hides the instruction: order here is a verb aimed at the letters, not at a supplier.
explanation.definitionFit: Become thinner -> RAREFY: to rarefy is to grow less dense, thinning out in substance the way mountain air does rather than in girth.

clue.text: Chinese toilet you're in starts to test everything

indicators.note: Something described as being in a word sits between its letters, so the piece named before this goes inside the pair that follows.

parts.note: the can is American slang for the lavatory

indicators.note: A word that is only starting to do something has got no further than its opening letter, and here two words in a row are docked to their firsts.

parts.note: its first letter alone
one's does duty for your in formal speech: one does one's best
the first letter again, closing the sandwich

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinese toilet' is there to make you picture plumbing. The pivot is 'you're': read it as the formal one's and it becomes the filling that two initials close around.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinese -> CANTONESE: definition by example, since Cantonese is one of the Chinese languages, the one spoken around Canton in the south.

clue.text: Route through grandstand is covered with beer

indicators.note: To be covered with something is to have it laid over you on every side, so the little word before this vanishes inside the drink named after it.

parts.note: ale is the standard three-letter beer, and it opens up after its first letter
the word is taken at face value and dropped straight in

explanation.walkthrough: Grandstands, beer and a route through them make one smooth picture, which is why 'is' reads as grammar rather than as two letters waiting to be used.
explanation.definitionFit: Route through grandstand -> AISLE: the gangway between blocks of seating, the walkway a spectator climbs to reach their row.

clue.text: Madonna covers numbers Rolling Stones worked on

indicators.note: A cover goes over the whole of what lies under it, so the woman named before this wraps right round the letters that follow.

parts.note: the Madonna is the Virgin Mary, and she opens up after two letters

indicators.note: Letters set rolling go end over end, and the three named here come to rest in the opposite order to the one written.

parts.note: nos. is the everyday abbreviation for numbers, and it goes in turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling Stones' is the trap: the eye takes the band name whole, and the clue splits it, keeping 'Rolling' for the wordplay and handing 'Stones' to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stones worked on -> MASONRY: masonry is stone that a mason has cut, dressed and laid, so it is precisely stone that has been worked.

clue.text: Army doctor shifted hips down a bit

indicators.note: Hips that have been shifted are no longer where they started, and the four letters beside the word move exactly as much.

parts.note: MO is the Medical Officer, the doctor attached to a British army unit
the same four letters in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: A dance-floor surface, with 'shifted' pretending to describe the hips while quietly instructing the letters. MO is worth learning: it turns up wherever a service doctor does.
explanation.definitionFit: down a bit -> MOPISH: mopish means dejected and listless, the mood of somebody moping about the place — low, though not desperately so.

clue.text: Travel writer back from Cairo cut old stuff up

indicators.note: A down entry is written from the top, so a piece said to go up it is read the other way round.
The back of a word is the letter it finishes on, so only the final character of the city named after it is wanted.

parts.note: the last letter of the city's name
to lop is to cut something off, usually a branch
O is the standard abbreviation for old
to cram a bag is to stuff it full

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a traveller's itinerary, so 'back from Cairo' reads as a journey home rather than as an instruction to keep one letter. O for old is worth pocketing.
explanation.definitionFit: Travel writer -> MARCO POLO: the Venetian merchant whose account of his years on the road to China is the founding book of the genre.

clue.text: E.g. stud to sleep with queen

parts.note: to poke is coarse slang for having sex with somebody
R is Regina, the Latin queen stamped on British coins and postboxes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about horses, where a stud is a breeding stable. Keep 'e.g.' in mind wherever it appears: it warns that the words after it name only an instance.
explanation.definitionFit: E.g. stud -> POKER: definition by example — stud poker is one form of the game, so the clue names a variety and wants the family.

clue.text: Cooking nerd used clove

indicators.note: Ingredients that are cooking are being stirred together into something other than what went in, and the letters beside the word get the same treatment.

parts.note: eight letters spanning the two words, to be reassembled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clove' looks like the spice sitting in a recipe, which is exactly what the kitchen surface wants. It is the last word of the clue and it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: clove -> SUNDERED: clove is the past tense of cleave, to split apart, so both words describe something already broken in two.

clue.text: American backing Trump's third term in newspaper article — strange world

indicators.note: Whoever is backing you stands behind you, so the pair of letters this describes is placed last rather than first.
Count into the name and stop at the third character — which, in a name of five letters, is also its centre.

parts.note: the middle letter of the five

indicators.note: A term is a limit or an end point, as in the term of a lease, so it asks for the letter the following word finishes on.

parts.note: the last letter of the word
an is the indefinite article used before a vowel
US does duty for the United States and for anything American

explanation.walkthrough: A clue full of political news, none of which matters: 'third' and 'term' are two separate instructions rather than the phrase they pretend to make together.
explanation.definitionFit: strange world -> URANUS: world in the sense of another planet, and strange because it is not ours — the seventh one out from the sun.

clue.text: Half undressed man checked out

indicators.note: Half of a word is what you keep and the rest is thrown away; here the front four characters of an eight-letter word survive.

parts.note: undressed is stripped, and only the front half of that eight-letter word is taken
the man who gets checked is the chess piece the whole game turns on

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the single word at the very end, which is what lets the rest run on as an ordinary sentence. Workers who are out have downed tools.
explanation.definitionFit: out -> STRIKING: 'out' in the union sense — a workforce out on strike is striking, and either word fits a sentence about a stoppage.

clue.text: Mop tea from cups

indicators.note: To cup something is to hold it between your hands, so the words in front of this are holding a run of letters between them.

parts.note: four consecutive letters here, running across the gap between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: A four-letter answer in a five-word clue leaves nowhere to hide, so the run has to straddle a word break — the one place the reading eye slides straight over.
explanation.definitionFit: Mop -> AFRO: a mop is a thick unruly head of hair, and the hairstyle is a round mass of exactly that.

clue.text: Irish writer on a bender beginning to imagine novel

indicators.note: A word that is only beginning to do something has got no further than its opening character, which is all the setter takes from it.
Novel means new and unfamiliar, so the letters are wanted in an arrangement nobody has seen yet — and it nods at the trade of the person defined.

parts.note: nine letters across three words, to be reassembled
its first letter, joining the other nine

explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' sits at the end doing two jobs at once: it is the signal that letters move, and it quietly tells you what the woman being defined wrote for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish writer -> EDNA O'BRIEN: the County Clare novelist whose The Country Girls was banned at home in 1960 — Irish by birth and by subject.

clue.text: English really get mushy about love at times

indicators.note: To go about a thing is to wrap round it, so the word before this closes over the single letter named after it.

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
really and very are interchangeable intensifiers: really good, very good
to soften is to go mushy, and this word opens up after its first letter
love is nil in tennis, written on the scoreboard as a nought

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sentimental Englishman, and every word of it is doing a second job. Love for O comes from tennis, where a nought is the score you dread.
explanation.definitionFit: at times -> EVERY SO OFTEN: the phrase means now and then, at irregular intervals — occasionally rather than to any schedule.

clue.text: Doctor came in GTi without an obvious explanation

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it until it is no longer what it was, which is what happens to the nine letters beside the word.

parts.note: nine letters, counting the three of the car badge, to be reassembled

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' opens the clue looking like the subject of a sentence about a man arriving in a hot hatch, and it is the instruction. GTi is a sporty trim badge.
explanation.definitionFit: without an obvious explanation -> ENIGMATIC: an enigma is a puzzle that resists solving, so anything enigmatic withholds the account you are after.

clue.text: Putting feathers on lady's head, going to get clips

indicators.note: A clip grips whatever is put into it, so the word this describes closes on the single letter and holds it inside.

parts.note: going to get something is fetching it, and the word opens up after its first letter
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clips' reads as a noun in the surface — film clips, hair clips — and it is really a verb, telling one word to take hold of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting feathers on -> FLETCHING: fletching is the trade word for fixing flight feathers to an arrow's shaft, from the old name for an arrow-maker.

clue.text: Landscape painter introduced to father, or rather mother

indicators.note: Introducing one person to others puts them right in among them, so the two letters before this go inside the group that follows.

parts.note: pa is the familiar word for a father
the phrase is the clue correcting itself in mid-sentence, and the word of refusal you say when you do that is the piece wanted
RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's standard painter
ma is the familiar word for a mother

explanation.walkthrough: The middle of the clue is a self-correction: father, then a refusal, then mother. The refusal is a word in its own right, and it supplies the letters between the two parents.
explanation.definitionFit: Landscape -> PANORAMA: an unbroken view of scenery stretching all round, which is landscape in the sense of a prospect rather than a painting.

clue.text: Greek character returned call in full pub

indicators.note: An across entry runs left to right, so a piece that has returned along it is written the other way about.
Sitting in a word means sitting between its letters, so everything named before this drops into the middle of what comes after.

parts.note: the whole of a thing is all of it, and this word splits after its first letter
eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet, and it goes in backwards
to ring somebody is to call them on the telephone

explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces go into the gap rather than one, and the definition is the last word standing alone. 'In full' reads as a phrase and is really two separate instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: pub -> WATERING HOLE: the animals' drinking place at the river, borrowed as a jokey name for where people go to drink.

clue.text: Dolphin swims up Margate's harbours on the ebb

indicators.note: To harbour something is to shelter it out of sight, which is what the words in front of it are doing with a run of letters.
An ebbing tide runs back out the way it came in, so the letters are taken in the opposite direction to the clue.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters here, read from the far end backwards and spanning two word breaks

explanation.walkthrough: The seaside surface does a lot of work: Margate is a Kent resort with a harbour, so 'harbours' reads as a noun until the moment you need it as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolphin -> GRAMPUS: a grampus is Risso's dolphin, the blunt-nosed grey species — an old sailors' name still used for the animal.

clue.text: Trouble that you have to step across climbing ornate tower

indicators.note: In a down entry the letters run downwards, so a piece climbing the column is written from the bottom up and reads backwards.

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble, as in much ado about nothing

parts.words: that you have to step across
parts.note: a gap in the ground is exactly the thing you have to step over

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' and the long phrase after it are both clued straight; the only cryptic instruction in the clue is 'climbing', and it applies to the pair of them at once.
explanation.definitionFit: ornate tower -> PAGODA: the many-tiered temple tower of east Asia, carved and decorated at every storey and built purely to be looked at.

clue.text: Prisoners' tea mum arranged, complete with relations

indicators.note: A mum who has arranged something has put it into an order of her own choosing, and the six letters beside the word are re-ordered too.

parts.note: a con is a convict, so prisoners are cons
six letters across the two words, reassembled

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue, and it is the marriage sense of the verb: a marriage is consummated when the couple first sleep together.
explanation.definitionFit: complete with relations -> CONSUMMATE: to consummate a marriage is to complete it by having sex, the one sense where completion and relations meet.

clue.text: Retailer's exchanges left in envelopes to be returned

indicators.note: Left in something is left inside it, so the letter named before this word sits between the letters of what comes after.

parts.note: an SAE is a stamped addressed envelope, the one you enclose so a reply can be posted back to you; more than one is SAEs
L is left, the standard abbreviation on maps and in stage directions

explanation.walkthrough: 'To be returned' is not an instruction to turn anything round: it is the part of the phrase that makes an envelope a stamped addressed one.
explanation.definitionFit: Retailer's exchanges -> SALES: a shop's sales are its transactions, goods handed over for money — the counting sense, not the January reductions.

clue.text: Half of fans in restaurant? More

indicators.note: Half of a word is the part you keep; the setter drops the rest, and here the first five characters of a ten-letter word are what stay.

parts.note: the fans that clear the air over a restaurant cooker are its extractors, and only the front half of that ten-letter word is kept

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fans' wants to be a crowd of supporters. The question mark is the setter flagging that the fans he means are the extractor fans in a restaurant kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: More -> EXTRA: something described as extra is added beyond what was counted on, so this is more in the sense of an additional amount.

clue.text: Duck after spies see you in Rome

indicators.note: A thing that comes after another is written second, so the piece named first in the sentence ends up last in the entry.

parts.note: the CIA is the American foreign intelligence service
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, written on the card as a nought

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is where duck means nought, from duck's egg — the round nothing beside a batsman's name. It is one of the commonest single-letter conventions in these puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: see you in Rome -> CIAO: the Italian for both hello and goodbye, so it is exactly what a Roman says on parting.

clue.text: Legless board work on drug dose

indicators.note: In an across clue one thing on another has been laid down after it, so the piece named first here is written second.

parts.note: a tablet is a measured dose of a drug, pressed into a pill
op is short for opus, a composer's work, as in Op. 27

explanation.walkthrough: 'Legless' does double duty: in the surface it means drunk, and in the definition it means exactly what it says, the flat part with the legs taken off.
explanation.definitionFit: Legless board -> TABLE TOP: the flat slab of a table, which is a board, and which is precisely the table minus its four legs.

clue.text: Fitter batters you'd expect to make fewer runs otherwise

parts.words: batters you'd expect to make fewer runs
parts.note: in cricket the tail is the last few batsmen in the order, picked for their bowling and not expected to score
or is the everyday alternative: this, or otherwise that

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitter' looks like a comparative — more fit — and is really a trade, somebody who fits things, which is what lets the definition sit at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitter -> TAILOR: a tailor's whole trade is fitting cloth to a body, so fitter names the job rather than describing better health.

clue.text: Parking behind college a considerable distance

parts.note: P is the sign on a parking space
the behind is the backside, and arse is the blunt British word for it
C is the abbreviation for college in names like Trinity C

explanation.walkthrough: A clue that reads as a note about the campus car park is really two abbreviations with a rude word between them — the joke the smooth surface is hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: a considerable distance -> PARSEC: the astronomer's unit of about 3.26 light years, used for the gaps between stars, so a very long way indeed.

clue.text: Forcibly make a sailor dangle aloft, caught on spar's tip

indicators.note: What you catch of a remark is its sound rather than its spelling, so the word beside this is wanted for how it is said.
In an across clue a piece resting on another has been laid down after it, so the letter clued last is written first.

parts.note: the tip of a word is its first letter, and a spar is a ship's mast or boom
to hang is to dangle from something, suspended by one end
aloft means high up, in the rigging of a ship, and the sound of that word is spelt out here in three quite different letters

explanation.walkthrough: The nautical surface is the point: it is exactly the world the definition comes from, where a man could be drugged in a port bar and wake up crewing a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Forcibly make a sailor -> SHANGHAI: to shanghai somebody is to drug or trick them into serving as crew, a press-gang trade named after the port.
